title: 1MW No. 324: The Advantage AI Can’t Give You
author: Greg McKeown
summary: In this 1-Minute Wednesday issue, Greg McKeown argues that as AI removes the friction from doing almost anything, the scarce advantage shifts from speed to discernment about what is worth doing. He observes that effort once imposed a natural speed limit that gave people time to judge whether an idea deserved to be pursued, and that universal speed is no advantage when everyone has it. He cites the 2025 Carnegie Mellon and Microsoft survey of 319 knowledge workers across 936 uses of generative AI, which associated greater confidence in AI with less critical thinking, but highlights its subtler finding that thinking moved toward evaluating, integrating and deciding what to do with AI output. His conclusion is that direction becomes more valuable as speed becomes common, and that the goal is to know what matters and then make that effortless. The issue ends with a three-step practice: ask AI for three distinct options with trade-offs, evaluate them, and act on the one that deserves effort.
points: McKeown frames the friction of effort as a hidden benefit that once forced people to decide whether an idea was worth doing.
He cites the Lee et al. 2025 study linking higher confidence in AI with reduced critical thinking among knowledge workers.
The study's more important finding, in his reading, is that thinking shifted toward evaluating and integrating AI output rather than disappearing.
His practical routine asks AI for three distinct options with trade-offs so that the human judgment step stays explicit.
quotes: The easier it becomes to do almost anything, the more valuable it becomes to know what is worth doing.
That friction can be frustrating, but it also gives us something that's easy to overlook: the time to decide whether the idea deserves to be done in the first place.
Contrast that with our AI-driven world where we can pursue literally any idea at a speed that was, until recently, unimaginable.
The original AI advantage was thought to be speed, but it is actually speed plus discernment.

Researchers at Carnegie Mellon and Microsoft asked 319 knowledge workers about 936 real uses of generative AI. The study found that greater confidence in AI was associated with less critical thinking.
The study showed that as AI took on more of the production, people shifted more of their thinking toward evaluating the output, integrating it, and deciding what to do with it
In the age of AI, a Signalist understands that the goal isn't to make everything effortless. It's to know what matters—and then make that effortless.
